The error handler accepts any type of error and shows its message directly.
Error handling and the redirect check are in place.

terms.meaning: Sending the user to a different page automatically, here to the page they wanted before signing in.
A reusable piece of logic that handles signing in and knowing who is signed in.
A web address path that the app knows how to show, such as the industries page.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports for the login page
sections.what: Brings in the React state tools, the auth hook, routing tools, icons, and the helper that builds asset addresses.
sections.why: Needed for the form state, the sign-in call, and the photo and icons on the page.

sections.name: getRedirect
sections.title: Reading the redirect destination
sections.what: Reads the redirect value from the address and returns it only if it is an in-app path other than the home page or the login page. Otherwise it returns the home page.
sections.why: Lets the user return to the page they were trying to open, while blocking redirects to outside sites.
sections.watch_out: Loosening this check could let the login page send users to outside addresses.

sections.name: Login (part 1)
sections.title: Sign-in logic and state
sections.what: Keeps the username, password, error, and loading state. When the form is submitted, it calls the login function and then sends the user onward. If login fails, it shows the error text.
sections.why: Connects the form to the auth hook and handles both success and failure.
sections.watch_out: Static Beacon pages are sent with a full page change, not the in-app router, so they must keep using the special branch.

sections.name: Login (part 2)
sections.title: Sign-in form fields and button
sections.what: Shows a red error box when there is an error, then username and password inputs and a submit button. The button is off until both fields have text, and shows a spinner with a waiting message during sign-in.
sections.why: Gives the user clear input fields and feedback while the sign-in request runs.
sections.watch_out: The button only checks that the fields are not empty, so the real check happens on the server.

sections.name: Login (part 3)
sections.title: Page footer and layout
sections.what: Shows a note telling the user to use the account created with a local setup command, and closes the page layout. It also shows a back link on the top of the page.
sections.why: Tells the user where the login account comes from during local setup.
sections.watch_out: The note names a local setup command, so it is only correct for local environments.

summary: This is the sign-in page where a user enters a username and password, and then goes to the page they originally asked for.
purpose: Lets a person prove who they are so they can use the protected workspace.
why: Protected pages need a signed-in user, so visitors are sent here first. The redirect keeps their place.
how: The user types a username and password. Submitting calls the login function from the auth hook. On success, the page reads the redirect value from the address and either opens a static Beacon page or moves to the route inside the app. On failure, it shows the error message.
inputs: The username and password typed by the user, and an optional redirect value in the page address.
outputs: A signed-in session through the auth hook, a redirect to the chosen page, or an error message on the page.
risks: The redirect value is taken from the address, so the code must keep accepting only in-app paths. The error message shown is whatever the login function throws.
debug: If sign-in fails, check the login function in the auth hook and the message it throws. If the user lands on the wrong page after sign-in, check the redirect value in the address. If the button stays disabled, check that both fields have text.
